mainTopic: The warning to witnesses in capital cases, testimony from guesswork (אומד), the snake that killed a murderer, teachings about קין and הבל, and how much גלות atones for.
overview: The משנה finishes the court's warning to witnesses in capital cases: do not hold back true testimony, and do not feel guilty when a wicked person dies. The גמרא explains that testimony from guesswork (אומד) is worth nothing, even when the evidence is overwhelming. רבי שמעון בן שטח tells how he saw such a case and could not convict, and the murderer was then killed by a snake. The גמרא asks why a murderer would die by a snake, since the דין of the four court deaths still brings a matching death. It answers that he also deserved burning for another sin, and the harsher death wins. The גמרא then tests whether the משנה allows אומד in money cases, like רבי אחא, and shows from hearsay (עד מפי עד) that the warning proves nothing. Next come teachings about קין and הבל, and a disagreement about how much גלות atones for: half a sin, three kinds of death, or everything. רבי יוחנן proves his view from King יכניה, whose son was born after his exile, and the explanation of that birth continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Witnesses must not hold back, and need not feel guilty
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends the court's warning to witnesses with two encouragements. Hiding testimony is a sin, and the death of a wicked person is cause for joy, not guilt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why should we get involved in this trouble? But the Torah already said that a witness who does not tell what he knows carries sin. And maybe you will say: why should we be responsible for this man's death? But the פסוק says: when the wicked are destroyed, there is joyful song.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes the speech the court gives to witnesses in a capital case. After scaring them so they will not lie, the court now makes sure they do not refuse to testify at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier warning was very frightening, so a witness might decide to stay silent. The court answers two worries. Staying silent is itself a sin (ויקרא 5:1), and if the defendant is truly guilty, his death is no tragedy (משלי 11:10).

keyTerms.meaning: 'and he is a witness', the פסוק requiring a witness to testify
to be guilty for someone's blood (his death)
'when the wicked perish, there is joyful song'

steps.whatToRemember: The court warns witnesses not to lie, but also not to stay silent. True testimony is a duty, even in a capital case.
steps.confusionAlert: The court is not trying to stop witnesses from testifying. The scary warning is aimed only at false or careless testimony.

phrases.english: Why should we get involved in this trouble?
But has it not already been stated:
"And he is a witness, whether he saw or knew,
if he does not tell, etc."
And perhaps you will say:

phrases.aramaic: מָה לָנוּ לָחוּב בְּדָמוֹ שֶׁל זֶה?
phrases.english: Why should we be responsible for this person's blood?
But has it not already been stated:
"When the wicked perish, there is joyful song."

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לָנוּ וְלַצָּרָה הַזֹּאת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה's warning to witnesses, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses must give true testimony even in capital cases. Withholding it is a sin, and the guilty party's death is not their fault.

steps.title: What counts as testimony from guesswork
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains the משנה's term אומד (guesswork). Even a chase, a bloody sword and a dying victim count as 'nothing' if the witnesses did not see the killing itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: what is testimony from guesswork? The court says to the witnesses: maybe this is what you saw. He ran after another man into a ruin, you ran after him, you found a sword in his hand dripping blood, and the victim was twitching. If that is all you saw, you saw nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by quoting a ברייתא that explains one word from the משנה's warning: testimony 'מאומד', from estimation or guesswork.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The example is as strong as circumstantial evidence can get, and the case is built that way on purpose. The point is that in capital cases, witnesses must see the act itself. Drawing a conclusion, however obvious, is not testimony.

keyTerms.meaning: the Talmud's discussion of the משנה
writhing, twitching (in the throes of death)

steps.whatToRemember: In a capital case, even overwhelming circumstantial evidence ('אומד') is not valid testimony. The witnesses must see the act.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the extremely high standard of proof for בית דין in capital cases. The next story shows this standard applied in real life.

phrases.english: Gemara: The Rabbis taught:
How is "from estimation" described?
He says to them: Perhaps this is what you saw?
That he ran after his fellow into a ruin,
and you ran after him,
and you found a sword in his hand
with its blood dripping,
and the murdered man was writhing.

phrases.aramaic: אִם כָּךְ רְאִיתֶם – לֹא רְאִיתֶם כְּלוּם.
phrases.english: If this is what you saw, you saw nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כֵּיצַד מֵאוֹמֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא by defining a term from the משנה's warning to witnesses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Testimony built on circumstantial evidence, even very strong evidence, is not accepted in capital cases.

steps.title: רבי שמעון בן שטח saw it happen and could do nothing
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן שטח swears he once saw exactly the case from the ברייתא. He could not convict the man because there were not two witnesses to the act, and he left the punishment to Heaven. A snake then bit the murderer and he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן שטח said: may I not see the comfort of Israel if I did not see a man chase another into a ruin. I ran after him and saw a sword in his hand dripping blood, and the victim twitching. I said to him: wicked one, who killed this man, me or you? But what can I do? Your life is not in my hands, because the Torah requires two witnesses. God, who knows thoughts, will punish the killer. They did not leave the spot before a snake bit the man and he died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a true story that matches the ברייתא's example exactly. It shows the rule in action: even a great judge could not convict.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story proves the rule is followed even when everyone 'knows' who did it. רבי שמעון בן שטח was a witness, but not to the killing itself, so the Torah's demand for עדים blocked a conviction. Heaven then punished the murderer directly.

keyTerms.meaning: an oath: 'may I (not) see the consolation of Israel' if this is not true
your blood (life) is not handed over to me, so I have no power to punish you
by the testimony of two witnesses
the One Who knows thoughts, meaning God

steps.confusionAlert: רבי שמעון בן שטח was not unsure who the killer was. He was sure, but certainty without eyewitnesses to the act is not enough for בית דין.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן שָׁטַח:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach said:
May I see consolation
phrases.notes: This is an oath. He means 'may I not see the comfort of Israel' if what follows is untrue.

phrases.english: if I did not see someone
who ran after his fellow into a ruin,
and I ran after him
and I saw a sword in his hand
with its blood dripping, and the murdered man writhing.
And I said to him: Wicked one,

phrases.aramaic: מִי הֲרָגוֹ לָזֶה? אוֹ אֲנִי אוֹ אַתָּה.
phrases.english: who killed this man? Either I or you.
But what can I do,
since your blood is not handed over to me,
for the Torah said:
"By the mouth of two witnesses shall the one who is to die be put to death."
The One Who knows thoughts

phrases.aramaic: יִפָּרַע מֵאוֹתוֹ הָאִישׁ שֶׁהָרַג אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ.
phrases.english: will punish that man who killed his fellow.
They said: They did not move from there
until a snake came and bit him, and he died.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן שָׁטַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life example of the exact case the ברייתא described.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that circumstantial evidence ('אומד') cannot convict in capital cases.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי שמעון בן שטח's sworn account of a murder he saw everything around but not the act, so he could not convict.

steps.title: Is a snake bite a fitting death for this murderer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the story's ending: should a murderer die by a snake? It brings רב יוסף and the school of חזקיה, who taught that the four court deaths never stopped even after the חורבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this man fit to die by a snake? But רב יוסף said, and the school of חזקיה also taught: from the day the בית המקדש was destroyed, even though the סנהדרין stopped working, the four death penalties did not stop.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the snake ending of the story. It brings a teaching that the four court death penalties continue even without a בית דין, which suggests the murderer should have died in a way that matches his sentence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If Heaven still carries out the four court deaths, a person should die in a way that matches the death he deserved. A murderer's sentence is the sword (הריגה), so a snake bite looks like the wrong match. Step 7 spells out the matching deaths, and Step 8 answers the question.

keyTerms.meaning: 'fit for a snake', deserving death by snake bite
the סנהדרין, the high court that judged capital cases
the four types of court-imposed death penalty

phrases.english: But is this man fit for a snake?
phrases.notes: In other words: is death by snake bite the right punishment for a murderer?

phrases.english: But didn't Rav Yosef say,
and so the school of Chizkiyah taught:
From the day the Temple was destroyed,
even though the Sanhedrin ceased,
the four death penalties did not cease.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַאי בַּר נָחָשׁ הוּא? וְהָאָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the ending of רבי שמעון בן שטח's story.
steps.kashyaTarget: The story's claim that the murderer died by a snake bite.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the four court deaths continue after the חורבן, a murderer should die in a way that matches his sentence, and a snake bite does not seem to fit.

steps.title: But the death penalties did stop
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pauses to question רב יוסף's wording: how can he say the four deaths did not stop, when courts no longer carry them out?
steps.simpleTranslation: They did not stop? But they did stop!
steps.whatsHappening: Before going on, the גמרא challenges the wording of the teaching it just quoted. As a plain fact, courts no longer put people to death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without a סנהדרין there is no court to sentence or execute anyone. So the words 'the four deaths did not stop' cannot be meant literally, and the גמרא asks what they do mean.

phrases.english: They did not cease? But they did cease!

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא בָּטְלוּ? וְהָא בָּטְלוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of רב יוסף's teaching quoted in the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's statement that the four deaths did not cease.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In reality, no court carries out executions anymore, so the statement seems false if read literally.

steps.title: The law of the four deaths still applies
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רב יוסף meant the דין of the four deaths has not stopped. Heaven still brings about a matching death, even though courts do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the law of the four death penalties did not stop.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question by adding one word: it is the 'דין' (law) of the four deaths that continues, not the court executions themselves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Courts no longer execute, but the person's sentence still exists, and Heaven carries out a matching form of death. This brings back the original question of why a murderer would die by a snake.
steps.whatToRemember: After the חורבן, the דין of the four deaths remains: Heaven brings a matching death, even without a court.
steps.whyThisMatters: This clarified principle is the basis for the question about the murderer's snake bite, which the גמרא goes on to resolve.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, דִּין אַרְבַּע מִיתוֹת לֹא בָּטְלוּ.
phrases.english: Rather, the law of the four death penalties did not cease.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, דִּין אַרְבַּע מִיתוֹת לֹא בָּטְלוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording challenge by reading the teaching as referring to the law, not the court executions.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It sounded like court executions literally still happen.
steps.terutzMaskana: The legal sentence of the four deaths remains in force and is carried out by Heaven, even though courts no longer execute.

steps.title: Which natural death matches each court death
steps.stepSummary: The teaching of רב יוסף and the school of חזקיה continues. It lists how Heaven carries out each of the four deaths: סקילה, שריפה, הריגה and חנק.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who deserves stoning either falls from a roof or is mauled by a wild animal. One who deserves burning either falls into a fire or is bitten by a snake. One who deserves the sword is either handed over to the government or attacked by robbers. One who deserves strangling either drowns in a river or dies of a choking throat illness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the 'matching death' idea from Step 6, one by one. Notice that a snakebite is listed under burning, not under the sword.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each natural death looks like its court death: a fall is like stoning, fire is like burning, a sword is like הריגה, and choking is like strangling. A murderer's court death is הריגה, so he should be killed by the government or by robbers. That brings back the question from Step 4: why did רבי שמעון בן שטח's murderer die from a snake?

keyTerms.meaning: Stoning, one of the four court deaths
Burning, one of the four court deaths
Death by the sword, the court death for a murderer
Strangling, one of the four court deaths
A throat illness that chokes a person (diphtheria)

steps.confusionAlert: This list does not answer the question about the snake. It actually makes the question stronger, because the snake appears under burning and not under the sword.

phrases.english: One who became liable to stoning –
either he falls from the roof,
or a wild animal mauls him.
One who became liable to burning –
either he falls into a fire,
or a snake bites him.
One who became liable to the sword –
either he is handed over to the government,
or robbers come upon him.
One who became liable to strangling –
either he drowns in a river,
or he dies of a choking throat illness.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי שֶׁנִּתְחַיֵּיב סְקִילָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the 'דין of four deaths' that Step 6 explained, and so renews the question about the snake from Step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each court death has natural matches: סקילה is a fall or a mauling, שריפה is fire or a snakebite, הריגה is the government or robbers, and חנק is drowning or a choking illness.

steps.title: The murderer had another sin deserving burning
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the murderer in the story was also guilty of a sin that deserved שריפה. A person liable to two court deaths receives the harsher one.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: that man had another sin. As the Master said: one who is liable to two court deaths is judged with the harsher one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers why the murderer died by a snake. He also deserved burning for a different sin, so he got the burning-type death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that when someone deserves two court deaths, he receives the more severe one. The גמרא assumes burning is harsher than the sword. So Heaven gave him a burning-type death, the snakebite, and the story fits רב יוסף's teaching after all.

keyTerms.meaning: He is judged with the harsher punishment

steps.whatToRemember: The snake does not break the rule of matching deaths. The murderer deserved burning for another sin, and the harsher death wins.

phrases.english: They say:
That man had another sin in him,
as the Master said:

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁנִּתְחַיֵּיב שְׁתֵּי מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין –
phrases.english: One who became liable to two court deaths –
is judged with the harsher one.
phrases.notes: The גמרא takes for granted that burning is harsher than the sword. That is why the snake, a burning-type death, fits.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: הָהוּא חֵטְא אַחֲרִיתִי הֲוָה בֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the renewed question: why the murderer got a burning-type death instead of a sword-type death.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adds a fact about the case (a second sin) plus a known rule (the harsher death wins)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought a murderer must die only by a sword-type death, so the snake seemed wrong.
steps.terutzMaskana: He also deserved burning, which is harsher, so a snakebite was the right matching death.

steps.title: Does the משנה allow guesswork in money cases?
steps.stepSummary: Back to the משנה's word אומד. The גמרא infers that guesswork is ruled out only in capital cases, so it must be allowed in money cases, and it asks whose opinion this is.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'From guesswork,' etc. It is in capital cases that we do not judge by guesswork. That implies that in money cases we do. Whose opinion is this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and draws an inference from its wording. Then it asks which תנא holds that view, setting up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה warns witnesses against אומד specifically in דיני נפשות. The גמרא reads this as a hint that in דיני ממונות the court may rule on strong circumstantial evidence. Since not everyone holds this, the גמרא asks whose view the משנה follows.

keyTerms.meaning: Guesswork, a conclusion drawn from circumstances without seeing the act
We judge by estimation or guesswork
Like whom? Which Tanna holds this?

phrases.english: 'From guesswork,' etc.
It is in capital cases that we do not judge by guesswork,
but in money cases we do judge by guesswork.
Like whom?

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵאוֹמֶד וְכוּ׳. בְּדִינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת הוּא דְּלָא אָמְדִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the snake story and returns to analyzing the משנה's word אומד.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which Tanna holds that money cases may be decided by אומד?

steps.title: It follows רבי אחא's camel case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה follows רבי אחא. He rules that when a wild camel is found next to a dead camel, we assume the wild camel killed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It follows רבי אחא, as a ברייתא teaches. רבי אחא says: if a camel in heat was rampaging among the camels, and a camel was found killed beside it, it is clear that this one killed it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question by naming רבי אחא. It quotes his ruling as proof that he judges money cases by guesswork.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody saw the wild camel kill the other camel. Still, רבי אחא makes the owner responsible based only on the circumstances. That is אומד in a money case, which matches what the משנה hinted.

keyTerms.meaning: A camel in heat that is rampaging
It is clear, it is known

phrases.english: Like רבי אחא,
as it is taught in a ברייתא: רבי אחא says:
A camel in heat rampaging among the camels,
and a camel was found killed at its side –
it is clear that this one killed it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּרַבִּי אַחָא, דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי אַחָא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'כמאן' question of Step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה follows רבי אחא, who decides money cases by guesswork, as shown in his rampaging-camel ruling.

steps.title: The same reasoning would wrongly allow hearsay in money cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the inference of Step 9. The משנה also warns against עד מפי עד in capital cases, but another משנה clearly rejects hearsay even in money cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: But by your reasoning, the משנה's warning against hearsay in capital cases would imply that hearsay is allowed in money cases! But we learned: if a witness says, 'He told me that he owes him,' or 'So-and-so told me that he owes him,' he has said nothing. He must say, 'In front of us he admitted to him that he owes him two hundred zuz.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the way Step 9 read the משנה. The same reading would lead to a ruling we know is false. The next step spells out what this challenge proves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists both אומד and עד מפי עד as warnings in capital cases. If 'only in capital cases' meant 'allowed in money cases', then hearsay would be allowed in money cases too. But the משנה on 29a says hearsay testimony is worthless even in money matters, so the inference itself looks shaky.

keyTerms.meaning: But according to your own reasoning
Hearsay: a witness repeating what someone else told him
He has said nothing; his testimony does not count

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying hearsay is allowed in money cases. It is showing that hearsay is NOT allowed there, to prove that the 'only in capital cases' reasoning does not work automatically.

phrases.english: But according to your reasoning,
hearsay testimony, which the משנה teaches about,
is it only in capital cases that we do not accept it,
but in money cases we do accept it?
But didn't we learn in a משנה:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה earlier in our מסכת, on 29a.

phrases.aramaic: אִם אָמַר ״הוּא אָמַר לִי שֶׁאֲנִי חַיָּיב לוֹ״,
phrases.english: If a witness said, 'He told me, "I owe him,"'

phrases.aramaic: ״אִישׁ פְּלוֹנִי אָמַר לִי שֶׁהוּא חַיָּיב לוֹ״ –
phrases.english: or 'So-and-so told me that he owes him' –
he has said nothing,
unless he says, 'In front of us he admitted to him
that he owes him two hundred zuz.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיטַעְמָיךְ, עֵד מִפִּי עֵד דְּקָתָנֵי בְּדִינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת הוּא דְּלָא אָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference from the משנה's wording that Steps 9 and 10 relied on.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that 'not allowed in capital cases' means 'allowed in money cases'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same inference, applied to עד מפי עד in the same משנה, would allow hearsay in money cases. But the משנה on 29a explicitly rejects hearsay in money cases.
steps.whyThisMatters: It forces the גמרא to explain why the משנה lists warnings for capital cases that may also apply to money cases. It also tests whether the link to רבי אחא really holds.

steps.title: The warning about guesswork proves nothing about money cases
steps.stepSummary: Since the משנה warns about עד מפי עד in capital cases even though it is also invalid in money cases, the same can be true of אומד. The inference from Step 9 falls away.
steps.simpleTranslation: So we see that even though something is invalid in money cases, we still warn the witnesses about it in capital cases. Here too, even though guesswork is invalid in money cases, we warn them about it in capital cases.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge from Step 11 and draws the conclusion: the משנה's warning about אומד does not mean אומד is allowed in money cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 reasoned that if the warning is said only in capital cases, אומד must be fine in money cases. But hearsay is warned about only in capital cases, and it is invalid everywhere. So the warning is just extra caution for capital cases. The proof that the משנה follows רבי אחא is knocked down.

keyTerms.meaning: We say it to them (we warn the witnesses)

steps.whatToRemember: The warning to witnesses in capital cases can include things that are invalid in money cases too. It is about how serious the case is, not about what is allowed elsewhere.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not say אומד is allowed in money cases. It shows the משנה fits even the view that אומד is invalid in money cases too, so the משנה does not have to follow רבי אחא.

phrases.aramaic: אַלְמָא, אַף עַל גַּב דִּפְסִילִי בְּדִינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת,
phrases.english: So we see: even though they are invalid in money cases,
phrases.notes: "They" means hearsay witnesses, from the challenge in Step 11.

phrases.english: we still warn them about it in capital cases.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי, אַף עַל גַּב דִּפְסִילִי בְּדִינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת,
phrases.english: Here too: even though guesswork testimony is invalid in money cases,
we warn them about it in capital cases.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא, אַף עַל גַּב דִּפְסִילִי בְּדִינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the challenge of Step 11 and spells out its result.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The inference in Step 9 that אומד is valid in money cases, and with it the need to say the משנה follows רבי אחא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Being warned about only in capital cases does not mean something is allowed in money cases, as עד מפי עד shows.

steps.title: קין struck הבל many times
steps.stepSummary: Quoting the משנה's warning, רב יהודה בריה דרבי חייא teaches that קין gave הבל many wounds, because he did not know where life leaves the body, until he reached the neck.
steps.simpleTranslation: "You should know" and so on. רב יהודה son of רבי חייא said: This teaches that קין made many bruises and many wounds on his brother הבל, because he did not know where the soul leaves the body, until he reached his neck.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה's warning to witnesses, which mentions הבל's blood, and brings a teaching about how קין killed הבל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה uses the plural word "דמי" (bloods) for הבל. רב יהודה reads the plural as many separate wounds. קין kept striking in different places because no one had ever killed before, until he hit the neck.

keyTerms.meaning: You should know (the start of the משנה's warning)

phrases.english: "You should know," and so on.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא:
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda, son of Rabbi Chiya, said:
This teaches that Cain made on his brother Hevel
many bruises and many wounds,
phrases.notes: He learns this from the plural word "דמי" (bloods) in בראשית 4:10.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה יוֹדֵעַ מֵהֵיכָן נְשָׁמָה יוֹצְאָה,
phrases.english: because he did not know where the soul leaves the body,
until he reached his neck.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֱווּ יוֹדְעִים כּוּ׳. אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אומד discussion and starts on a new phrase in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The plural "דמי" shows that קין struck הבל many times before killing him at the neck.

steps.title: The earth never opened its mouth again
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה teaches that after the earth swallowed הבל's blood, it never opened its mouth again. He proves it from a פסוק that says songs come from the earth's "corner," not its "mouth."
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יהודה son of רבי חייא said: From the day the earth opened its mouth and took in הבל's blood, it never opened again, as it says: "From the corner of the earth we heard songs: glory to the righteous." From the corner of the earth, and not from the mouth of the earth.
steps.whatsHappening: A second teaching of רב יהודה about הבל: the earth opened its mouth once for his blood and never again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in ישעיהו says songs come from the "corner" of the earth. רב יהודה asks why it does not say "mouth". His answer is that the earth's mouth has stayed closed since it took in הבל's blood.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא:
phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda, son of Rabbi Chiya, said:
From the day the earth opened its mouth
and took in the blood of Hevel,
it never opened again,
as it says: "From the corner of the earth we have heard songs:
glory to the righteous."
From the corner of the earth, and not from the mouth of the earth.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching by the same אמורא on the same story of הבל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After taking in הבל's blood, the earth never opened its mouth again.

steps.title: But the earth opened its mouth for קרח
steps.stepSummary: His brother חזקיה challenges him with the פסוק about קרח: "And the earth opened its mouth."
steps.simpleTranslation: His brother חזקיה challenged him: But it says "And the earth opened its mouth"!
steps.whatsHappening: חזקיה challenges Step 14 with a פסוק showing the earth did open its mouth again, in the story of קרח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 said the earth never opened its mouth after הבל. But the earth clearly opened its mouth to swallow קרח and his group, long after הבל.

phrases.english: His brother Chizkiya challenged him:
"And the earth opened its mouth"!
phrases.notes: במדבר 16:32, where the earth swallowed קרח.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ חִזְקִיָּה אָחִיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the claim of Step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the earth never opened its mouth after הבל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק says the earth opened its mouth for קרח, so it did open again.

steps.title: It opened for bad, not for good
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה answers that the earth opened again only to punish, as with קרח. It never again opened to do good.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It opened for bad; it did not open for good.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers his brother's challenge by narrowing what he meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With קרח, the earth opened to punish. The פסוק of "songs" and "glory to the righteous" is about good things, and those never came from the earth's mouth again. So both פסוקים fit.

phrases.english: He said to him: For bad it opened;
for good it did not open.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לְרָעָה פָּתְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The earth never opened its mouth at all after הבל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The earth never again opened its mouth for good. It did open for punishment, as with קרח.

steps.title: גלות atones for half a sin
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה teaches that גלות atones for half a sin. He proves it from קין, who was first told he would be "נע ונד" but in the end was only "נוד".
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יהודה son of רבי חייא said: Exile atones for half a sin. At first it is written: "I will be a fugitive and a wanderer," and at the end it is written: "And he lived in the land of נוד."
steps.whatsHappening: A third teaching of רב יהודה about קין: going into גלות removes half of a sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קין was first punished with two things: "נע" (fugitive) and "נד" (wanderer). Later the פסוק mentions only "נוד", which is like "נד". Half the punishment fell away, so his גלות atoned for half the sin.
steps.whatToRemember: All three teachings of רב יהודה come from the story of קין and הבל: the many wounds, the earth's closed mouth, and גלות atoning for half a sin.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא:
phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda, son of Rabbi Chiya, said:
Exile atones for half a sin.
At first it is written: "And I will be a fugitive and a wanderer,"
and at the end it is written: "And he lived in the land of Nod."
phrases.notes: בראשית 4:16. "נוד" sounds like "נד", so only the wandering was left and the "נע" was gone.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא: גָּלוּת מְכַפֶּרֶת עָוֹן מֶחֱצָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third teaching by the same אמורא about the story of קין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גלות atones for half a sin, as shown by קין's punishment shrinking from "נע ונד" to only "נוד".

steps.title: Exile saves from three kinds of death
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה teaches that גלות atones for three things, meaning sword, famine and plague, based on a פסוק in ירמיהו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: Exile atones for three things, as it says: "So says ה׳: he who stays in this city will die by the sword, by famine, and by plague. But he who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who are besieging you will live, and his life will be his as a prize."
steps.whatsHappening: A different sage, רב יהודה (not רב יהודה בריה דרבי חייא from the earlier steps), gives his own view of what גלות atones for: going into exile can save you from three kinds of death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, staying in the city means dying in one of three ways: sword, famine or plague. Going out to the enemy and being exiled means you live. So גלות protects a person from all three of these deaths.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
Exile atones for three things,
as it is said: "So says ה׳, etc."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 21:8–9. The word וגו׳ ("etc.") means the גמרא skips some words of the פסוק.

phrases.english: he who stays in this city
will die by the sword, by famine, and by plague,
and he who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans
who are besieging you
will live, and his life will be his as a prize."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: גָּלוּת מְכַפֶּרֶת שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching about the power of גלות, from רב יהודה. He is a different אמורא from רב יהודה בריה דרבי חייא, who taught in the previous step that גלות atones for half a sin.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גלות saves a person from the three deaths of sword, famine and plague.

steps.title: Exile atones for everything: the curse on King יכניה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says גלות atones for everything. He starts his proof with the harsh curse on King יכניה that he would be childless and that none of his descendants would rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Exile atones for everything, as it says: "So says ה׳: Write this man down as childless, a man who will not succeed in his days. For no man of his offspring will succeed in sitting on the throne of דוד and ruling again in יהודה."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a bigger claim than רב יהודה: גלות atones for everything. He quotes the curse on יכניה to set up his proof, which comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה limited the power of גלות to three kinds of death, but רבי יוחנן says it wipes away everything. This first פסוק shows how severe יכניה's punishment was: no children, and no descendant on the throne of דוד. The next step will show that this curse was undone after his exile.

keyTerms.meaning: the throne of David, the kingship of Judah

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Exile atones for everything,
as it is said: "So says ה׳:
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 22:30. This פסוק is about King יכניה.

phrases.english: Write this man down as childless,
a man who will not succeed in his days,
for no man of his offspring will succeed
in sitting on the throne of David
and ruling again in Judah."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: גָּלוּת מְכַפֶּרֶת עַל הַכֹּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a broader view than רב יהודה: גלות atones for everything, not just three kinds of death.

steps.title: After his exile, יכניה has a son
steps.stepSummary: After יכניה was exiled, the פסוק lists his son. The curse of childlessness was removed, which proves that גלות atoned for him completely.
steps.simpleTranslation: And after he was exiled, it is written: "And the sons of יכניה: אסיר, שלתיאל his son."
steps.whatsHappening: This is the punchline of רבי יוחנן's proof. After יכניה went into exile, the פסוק speaks of his son, so he was no longer childless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יכניה had been cursed to be "childless." Yet once he was exiled, the פסוק lists his son שלתיאל. The curse was cancelled, which shows that גלות wiped away even such a severe decree.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's proof: יכניה was cursed to be childless, but after his exile he had a son. So גלות atoned for everything.

phrases.english: And after he was exiled, it is written:
"And the sons of Jeconiah: Assir,"
(his son) Shealtiel his son."
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some leave it out.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבָתַר דִּגְלָה כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי יוחנן's proof by showing that the curse from the previous step was undone after the exile.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's claim that גלות atones for everything.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברי הימים א 3:17, where יכניה's son is listed after his exile, despite the curse of childlessness.

steps.title: Explaining the names אסיר and שלתיאל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the son's names. אסיר means his mother conceived him in prison. שלתיאל means God "planted" him in an unusual way. It then starts to explain what was unusual, based on a tradition about conception.
steps.simpleTranslation: "אסיר": his mother conceived him in prison. "שלתיאל": God planted him in a way unlike the usual way things are planted. We have a tradition that a woman does not conceive while standing,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads hidden meanings into the names in the פסוק. It is setting up an explanation of the unusual birth that continues in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name אסיר comes from אסור, "prisoner," so the son was conceived while יכניה was in prison. The name שלתיאל is read as שתל + אל, "God planted," meaning he came about in an unusual way. The tradition that a woman does not conceive while standing is the first piece of explaining that miracle, and it continues in the next section.

keyTerms.meaning: things that are planted (here, people being born)

phrases.english: "Assir": that his mother conceived him
in prison.
"Shealtiel": that God planted him
phrases.notes: The name is read as two words: שתל ("planted") and אל ("God").

phrases.english: not in the usual way of those who are planted.
We have a tradition that a woman does not
conceive while standing,

steps.triggerLanguage: אַסִּר – שֶׁעִיבְּרַתּוּ אִמּוֹ בְּבֵית הָאֲסוּרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the names in the פסוק just quoted, showing how יכניה's son came to be born.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The names אסיר and שלתיאל show that the son was conceived in prison, in an unusual way brought about by God.
